                 REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

         Danay Covert, on behalf of Covert DCC Ranches LP #1 and #2, Kenny Covert, and Chance

Covert (collectively “Coverts”), and Rodger and Barbara Maddox (collectively “Maddoxes”)

submit these Joint Replies to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”).

                                      I.       SUMMARY OF REPLY

         If the Public Commission of Texas (“Commission”) reaches the issue of Routing Criteria, 1

the Coverts and Maddoxes support and urge the adoption of the PFD’s recommended route – Route

894. Route 894 may be the “the least bad option available” 2 considered in this proceeding given

the number of impacted landowners. But, Route 894 is the most credible route for a variety of

 reasons, including: it is the only proposed route that is supported by an end-to-end holistic

analysis of route and link alternatives. 3 With the exception of Commission Staff’s recommended

route (Route 487), all of the alternative route studies and analyses offered by various landowners’

consultants or experts are not end-to-end holistic analysis, as they either omit certain factors or use

a mathematical methodology designed to weigh the factors they need to achieve avoidance of their

respective clients’ properties. The PFD provides ample rationale and citations of record evidence

to support its recommendation of Route 894. 4

        The Coverts and Maddoxes object to and do not support Routes CCG5, 296 6, or any route

that uses Links J33, J6, and/or K41. These objectional routes move the transmission line to the

most southern corridor of the study area only to avoid the transmission lines crossing certain

landowner properties under the guise of result-oriented analyses. These three routes unnecessarily

cross the Coverts and Maddoxes working ranches and homesteads and, as the PFD did, these routes

should be rejected as viable alternatives.

                       II.     THE COVERTS AND MADDOXES’ INTERESTS

        The Coverts and the Maddoxes have working ranch operations located on the Southern

Corridor of the proposed routes that are impacted by Links J33, J6, and/or K41. These ranches are

not rolling farmland or some form of investments; they are working ranches that produce revenue

streams and are legacy properties that are family-owned and operated. Of importance to note:

    •   Covert DCC Ranches LP #1 and #2 7
           o The two ranches are contiguous to one another and cover 7,950 acres.
           o The two ranches’ operations are intertwined and are not divided by platted property
               boundaries.
           o The two ranches are detrimentally impacted by Links J33, J6, and K41.
           o The ranches collectively have 4 habitable structures, 5 barns, cattle, cattle pens,
               feeders, 10 acre release pens, hay and oat fields, traveling irrigations systems,
               wildlife, hunting areas, lakes, pond, water wells, and natural springs on the
               properties. 8

    •   Maddoxes Ranch 9
          o The Maddoxes’ ranch covers 998 acres and is impacted by Link J33.
          o The Maddoxes have lived on their ranch for over 50 years, and it is their homestead
             where they currently live and work.
          o The ranch has several attributes, including granite outcropping of granite hills and
             ledges, three habitable structures, barns, cattle and hunting operations, water wells
             and water bodies that provide water to the ranch as well as surrounding areas.
          o The Maddoxes’ ranch is their legacy to their sons and grandchildren.


        The Coverts and Maddoxes presented non-controverted 10 evidence about their properties

and the significant and detrimental impact of the 765 kV transmission line crossing their ranches.

However, they do not attempt to veil their objections to certain routes based “weighing” various

factors – but rather citing known reasons to oppose any route that included Links J33, J6, and K41:

        •   Fragmentation and Failure of Paralleling. Use of these three links will forever
            fragment and cause critical damage to the Coverts’ ranches. Based on the Oncor
            Intervenor Map, Links J33, J6, and K4 will cut the Covert ranches into two or three

             Coverts ranches in half causing a significant problem with operations and viability of
             the ranches because it apparently relies on platted property lines that in reality have no
             importance as to the use of these properties.

        •    Engineering Constraints. The Covert ranches have two travelling irrigation systems
             covering 42 acres and 15 acres, respectively to water their revenue-producing hay
             fields, with a third under construction. 12

        •    Environmental Integrity: Mr. Covert and Mrs. Maddox voiced concerns about the
             environmental impact of the construction and placement of the easements and towers
             on their respective properties – particularly as it relates to impact on cattle and deer,
             permanent destruction of natural vegetation, and likely impact on existing creeks, water
             ways, and natural springs. 13

        •    Aesthetic and Community Values. A study on this issue is not necessary – a 765 kV
             transmission line with structures that are up to 198 feet tall and approximately 140 feet
             wide set in a 200-foot wide easement will impact the aesthetics of any property. The
             lines and towers will become a visual blight on the ranches. 14

        •    Habitable Structures. Link J6 impacts one habitable structure on the Coverts ranch
             that is located within 180 yards from the centerline of the easement. 15 As Mrs. Maddox
             testified, it is unclear whether their house is within 200 feet of the center line of the J33
             as they received inconsistent responses from Oncor, so she remains concerned about
             the location of the easements. 16

        •    Impact on Electric Service and Costs. PURA requires consideration of the “probable
             improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers in the area” a proposed
             transmission line on electric service and costs to the utility’s customers. 17 This project
             is not being built to improve service or lower the electric costs of Covert, Maddox, or
             any landowner in this area; it is being built to deliver power to the Permian Basin
             Region. Oncor admits as much. 18


        From the Coverts and Maddoxes’ perspectives, direct impact and significant harm will

result if Links J6, J33, and/or K41 are used in the route approved by the Commission.

                               III.     ROUTE 894 SHOULD BE ADOPTED

          The PFD provides ample support of the credible evidence to support adoption of Route

894. This route was proposed by Oncor/LCRA as their Best Meets Route. 19 This route remains

the only end-to-end holistic analysis of route and link alternatives. 20 While some parties oppose

this route, there appears to be no dispute that the Applicants’ analysis is the only end-to-end holistic

approach where there is no allegation that the results of the analysis by Oncor/LCRA was result-

driven.

          The PFD identifies “key attributes” of Route 894 and compares those attributes to three

other routes (Routes 296, 392, and 487). The PFD narrows the focus to these four routes as the

“Focus Routes.” The PFD painstakingly addresses the “key” factors related to the Focus Routes,

as well as addresses other routes of interest. 21 The Coverts and Maddoxes submit that the PFD’s

analysis of the Focus Routes and other routes provides sufficient and defensible rationales to

support its recommendation of Route 894, while identifying key reasons that it does not

recommend adoption of the other three Focus Routes or other alternative routes.

          The Commission Staff’s recommended route, Route 487, is included in the Focus Routes.

The Coverts and Maddoxes do not oppose Route 487, primarily because Staff’s analysis did not

appear to be result-driven, but rather based on Staff Witness John Poole’s experience in reviewing

transmission line routes. The primary criticism of Staff’s proposed route is that Mr. Poole had not

completed his review and analysis of all landowners as of the time of filing its recommendation. 22

                   IV.       ROUTES OF INTEREST THAT SHOULD NOT BE
                                            ADOPTED

       The standard for review of the PFD’s detailed factual analysis of the record evidence is

that the Commission may modify the PFD, only if the parties filing Exceptions establish that the

PFD’s recommended findings of fact was not adequately supported or the PFD erroneously applied

PURA § 37.056 or the PUC Rules. With respect to Routing Criteria, the Exceptions filed seeking

an approval of a route other than Route 894 cite the same evidence and arguments submitted to

the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”). None of the Exceptions related to Routing Criteria

identify new evidence or arguments, but rather repeat the positions and evidence submitted to and

considered by the ALJs. The Coverts and Maddoxes respectfully suggest that the Commission

adopt the PFD’s recommendations on Routing as there is no basis to modify the findings of fact

or application of the law.

       The Coverts and Maddoxes oppose the following routes: Route 296 (Focus Route), Route

CCG, and any route that uses Links J33, J6 and/or K41. The analyses used to support these routes,

purportedly weigh certain statutory and regulatory factors using various numerical or analytical

methodologies, and result every time in proposing a route that does not cross their respective

landowners’ properties. The PFD accurately reflects the primary weaknesses of each of these

routes. There are two of these routes – 296 and CCG – that merit specific replies.

       A. Route 296 should not be adopted.

       The PFD got it right – Route 296 should not be adopted. The PFD correctly concludes that

Route 296 is not more favorable than Route 894 for the following reasons:



                                                6
      •   Route 296 is not Staff’s second alternative route. While Staff witness Pool originally
         considered this route as a “second choice” at the time of his deposition, after further review
         of additional evidence, Staff no longer considered Route 296 as an alternative route. 23

     •   Route 296 is no more favorable than Route 894 as it relates to impact on parks or
         recreational areas within 1,000 feet of the route’s centerline and is comparatively the same
         as Route 894 with respect to visual zones of parks/recreational areas. 24

     •   Route 296 costs approximately $20 million more than Route 894. 25

     •   Route 296 impacts more habitable structures than Route 894. 26


As the PFD properly notes, while Route 296 performed “favorably” on environmental

considerations, “it has considerable downsides.” 27 Of note is that the centerline of Route 296 runs

within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two (2) churches. While proponents of this

Route suggest that this part of Route 296 can be moved, there is no evidence in the record that

identifies the alternative route/link changes to achieve missing the school and churches without

adversely impacting other landowners or other structures. Therefore, there is no evidentiary basis

to determine if moving the impacted link is reasonable or meets the applicable law and rules.

         B. Route CCG should not be adopted.

         Route CCG is not one of the four Focus Routes, although the PFD correctly notes that

Oncor/LCRA identified Route CCG as a “route of interest.” 28 Importantly, the PFD correctly

concludes that Route CCG, as compared to the Focus Routes, did not present a “clear advantage”

over Route 894, particularly with respect to the costs and impact on habitable structures. 29

         Some context of the Route CCG will also provide insight as to how the evidentiary record

that supports rejection of Route CCG. Cherokee Creek Partners, along with other individual

landowners, (collectively “Cherokee Creek”) cobbled together several alternative routes using

links identified by Oncor/LCRA. They then sponsored the testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider

Reinecke 30 to identify and to support a route labelled “Cherokee Creek G” or “CCG”. In reaching

her recommendation, Ms. Reinecke used a quartile ranking system based on statistics and standard

deviations. 31

        The PFD rejects Route CCG and the PFD’s analysis and recommendations are supported

by credible evidence in the record for the following additional reasons:

     • Ms. Reinecke’s system methodology appears to be result-driven. Applicants’ Best-Meets
       Route 894 crosses segments of Ms. Reinecke’s clients’ properties. But after Ms.
       Reinecke’s analysis was completed, none of the CCG links cross the property owned by
       her clients. 32

     • Ms. Reinecke’s quartile ranking system or use of standard deviation has not been used or
       approved in any prior routing cases. 33

     • Ms. Reinecke’s system and analysis does not address costs as a factor. 34


     • Ms. Reinecke’s analysis considers “community values including public opinion as gauged
       using items filed in . . . Docket 59475.” 35 But it is clear that she did not consider opinions
       rendered by the Coverts, the Maddoxes or any landowner along the Southern Corridor or
       impacted by Links J6, J33 and K41.

      •   CCG crosses 55 more streams than Route 894; 36 it crosses 24 more FM County roads
         than Route 894; 37 and crosses more historical and high potential archeological areas. 38

     •   CCG costs approximately $40 million more than Route 894. 39

     •   CCG passes 20 more habitable structures than Route 894. 40

The Coverts and Maddoxes submit that neither of these two alternative routes should be adopted.


                        V.      CONCLUSION AND REQUESTED RELIEF

         In a case of this magnitude, there are no winners – except for Oncor/LCRA because they

will recover all of their costs from ratepayers, even if those ratepayers are not receiving any savings

or power from this project. Route 894 is the best choice supported by an end-to-end holistic

approach conducted by persons who have no “dog in the fight”. Route 894 is not perfect, but

based on the credible evidence, it is the “best” option. In contrast, the alternative routes such as

Route CCG or Route 296 are presented as weighing statutory and regulatory factors, but clearly

the weighing is intended to achieve a single purpose: to avoid their respective clients’ property.

         The Coverts and Maddoxes support Route 894 and oppose any route that includes use of

Links J6, J33, and/or K41, including Routes 296 and CCG. The Coverts and Maddoxes explain

their concerns and the likely impact on their properties – they know their land and the impact the

765 kV transmission line and 200 feet wide easement will have on their property and livelihoods.

In this case, given the plethora of proposed routes, the Commission should recognize the critical

analysis of the PFD on attributes of the various alternative routes and the PFD’s ultimate rejection

of all of the proposed routes, except for Route 894.

                                III.      ROUTE 894 SHOULD BE ADOPTED

          The PFD provides ample support of the credible evidence to support adoption of Route

894. This route was proposed by Oncor/LCRA as their Best Meets Route. 19 This route remains

the only end-to-end holistic analysis of route and link alternatives.20 While some parties oppose

this route, there appears to be no dispute that the Applicants' analysis is the only end-to-end holistic

approach where there is no allegation that the results of the analysis by Oncor/LCRA was result-

driven.

          The PFD identifies "key attributes" of Route 894 and compares those attributes to three

other routes (Routes 296, 392, and 487). The PFD narrows the focus to these four routes as the

"Focus Routes." The PFD painstakingly addresses the "key" factors related to the Focus Routes,

as well as addresses other routes of interest. 21 The Coverts and Maddoxes submit that the PFD' s

analysis of the Focus Routes and other routes provides sufficient and defensible rationales to

support its recommendation of Route 894, while identifying key reasons that it does not

recommend adoption of the other three Focus Routes or other alternative routes.

          The Commission Staff' s recommended route, Route 487, is included in the Focus Routes.

The Coverts and Maddoxes do not oppose Route 487, primarily because Staff' s analysis did not

appear to be result-driven, but rather based on Staff Witness John Poole' s experience in reviewing

transmission line routes. The primary criticism of Staff' s proposed route is that Mr. Poole had not

completed his review and analysis of alllandowners as ofthe time of filing its recommendation.22

                   IV.       ROUTES OF INTEREST THAT SHOULD NOT BE
                                                ADOPTED
       The standard for review of the PFD' s detailed factual analysis of the record evidence is

that the Commission may modify the PFD , only if the parties filing Exceptions establish that the

PFD' s recommended findings of fact was not adequately supported or the PFD erroneously applied

PURA § 37.056 or the PUC Rules. With respect to Routing Criteria, the Exceptions filed seeking

an approval of a route other than Route 894 cite the same evidence and arguments submitted to

the Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs"). None of the Exceptions related to Routing Criteria

identify new evidence or arguments, but rather repeat the positions and evidence submitted to and

considered by the ALJs. The Coverts and Maddoxes respectfully suggest that the Commission

adopt the PFD' s recommendations on Routing as there is no basis to modify the findings of fact

or application of the law.

       The Coverts and Maddoxes oppose the following routes: Route 296 (Focus Route), Route

CCG, and any route that uses Links J33, J6 and/or K41. The analyses used to support these routes,

purportedly weigh certain statutory and regulatory factors using various numerical or analytical

methodologies, and result every time in proposing a route that does not cross their respective

landowners' properties. The PFD accurately reflects the primary weaknesses of each of these

routes. There are two of these routes - 296 and CCG - that merit specific replies.

       A. Route 296 should not be adopted.

       The PFD got it right - Route 296 should not be adopted. The PFD correctly concludes that

Route 296 is not more favorable than Route 894 for the following reasons:




                                                6
     •   Route 296 is not Staff's second alternative route. While Staff witness Pool originally
         considered this route as a "second choice" at the time of his deposition, after further review
         of additional evidence, Staff no longer considered Route 296 as an alternative route. 23

    •   Route 296 is no more favorable than Route 894 as it relates to impact on parks or
         recreational areas within 1,000 feet ofthe route's centerline and is comparatively the same
         as Route 894 with respect to visual zones of parks/recreational areas.24

    •   Route 296 costs approximately $20 million more than Route 894.25

    •   Route 296 impacts more habitable structures than Route 894.26


As the PFD properly notes, while Route 296 performed "favorably" on environmental

considerations, "it has considerable downsides."27 Of note is that the centerline of Route 296 runs

within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two (2) churches. While proponents of this

Route suggest that this part of Route 296 can be moved, there is no evidence in the record that

identifies the alternative route/link changes to achieve missing the school and churches without

adversely impacting other landowners or other structures. Therefore, there is no evidentiary basis

to determine if moving the impacted link is reasonable or meets the applicable law and rules.

         B. Route CCG should not be adopted.

        Route CCG is not one of the four Focus Routes, although the PFD correctly notes that

concludes that Route CCG, as compared to the Focus Routes, did not present a "clear advantage"

over Route 894, particularly with respect to the costs and impact on habitable structures. 29

                       V.      CONCLUSION AND REOUESTED RELIEF

        In a case of this magnitude, there are no winners - except for Oncor/LCRA because they

will recover all oftheir costs from ratepayers, even ifthose ratepayers are not receiving any savings

or power from this proj ect. Route 894 is the best choice supported by an end-to-end holistic

approach conducted by persons who have no "dog in the fight"          Route 894 is not perfect, but

based on the credible evidence, it is the "best" option. In contrast, the alternative routes such as

Route CCG or Route 296 are presented as weighing statutory and regulatory factors, but clearly

the weighing is intended to achieve a single purpose: to avoid their respective clients' property.

        The Coverts and Maddoxes support Route 894 and oppose any route that includes use of

Links J6, J33, and/or K41, including Routes 296 and CCG. The Coverts and Maddoxes explain

their concerns and the likely impact on their properties - they know their land and the impact the

765 kV transmission line and 200 feet wide easement will have on their property and livelihoods.

In this case, given the plethora of proposed routes, the Commission should recognize the critical

analysis ofthe PFD on attributes ofthe various alternative routes and the PFD's ultimate rejection

of all of the proposed routes, except for Route 894.
